newsitem.title: USA: Does Lockheed-Northrop deal go too far?
newsitem.headline: Does Lockheed-Northrop deal go too far?

text.p: Will the combination of Lockheed Martin Corp. and Northrop Grumman Corp. be one merger too many in the shrinking defense industry?

Antitrust lawyers and stock market analysts pondered that on Thursday, after two survivors in the aerospace industry announced their intention to combine in an $11.6 billion deal that would narrow shopping choices for the U.S. military.

"I think this is inflammatory," said Steve Axinn, a New York antitrust lawyer with Axinn, Veltrop & Harkrider. "Even if these guys don't compete head-on, they are the most likely bidders on a variety of heavy-duty hardware" in the future.
But in the end, he said, it will probably be the Pentagon recommendation to antitrust authorities that determines the outcome of the merger.

For years since the end of the Cold War the military has encouraged defense contractors to get together, but in recent months both antitrust officials and the military have suggested there will be a day when enough is enough.

That day moved a bit closer this week, as competition officials approved two large aerospace deals -- Boeing Co. with McDonnell Douglas Corp. and Raytheon's purchase of Texas Instruments' defense electronics business.
Raytheon is continuing negotiations with the Justice Department on its proposed $9.5 billion takeover of Hughes Electronics Corp.'s defense business.

"Both of these will be under, I would guess, rather severe regulatory review between now and the end of the year," Paul Nesbit of JSA Research in Newport, R.I., said of the Raytheon and Lockheed proposals.
Still, stock analysts say that with one glaring exception there is little overlap between Lockheed and Northrop now.

They say the companies will likely face divestiture in the lucrative area of electronic countermeasures -- the ability of airplanes to send false signals that foil the radar on incoming air-to-air missiles and dozens of other ways of fooling the enemy.

"They each have a half-billion dollars in electronic countermeasures," said Roger Threlfall, an analyst for J.P. Morgan. "The nearest competitor is Litton ITT," which is far smaller. One potential purchaser would be Raytheon, which has an interest in the area but not a large presence compared to the leaders, he said.
In Threlfall's view, the fact that both companies make fighter aircraft does not amount to an overlap.

Northrop is an important participant in the FA-18, a Navy fighter slated for 550 to 785 planes at a cost of about $35 million each, he said. Lockheed is the builder of the F-22 next-generation superiority fighter for the Air Force, and will sell 339 planes at about $80 million each.
"I would say aircraft is not even an issue," Threlfall said, because the two programs are complementary.
Lior Bregman of Oppenheimer & Co. agreed, saying that the two companies were getting together "to acquire a critical mass" in aircraft.

And while both work in the area of command, control, communications and intelligence, Northrop makes an airplane that helps map out what is happening on the ground while Lockheed makes ground components that help combatants stay in touch with each other.
Nonetheless, in the end no one knows exactly what the government will do.

"The Department of Defense wants competition so they're not subject to a monopoly," said Lawrence Stern, a research professor at George Mason University's Institute of Public Policy. "The key point is, how few firms can they have? If you have too few firms, then you become a captive and you lose the vitality of new ideas" fostered by competition, he said.
Lockheed's stock fell $4.875 to $99.125, while McDonnell Douglas slid 31 cents to $70.19 on the New York Stock Exchange. Northrop's stock rose $21.125 to $110, also on NYSE.
